evidence: Hor. S. 1.1.96: ita sordidus, ut sē nōn umquam servō melius vestīret (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: First “dirty”, then “mean, niggardly” (Lewis & Short), of the miser in Horace who dressed no better than his slave.

evidence: Prop. 3.17.18: astrictus pater (Lewis & Short s.v. astringō)
terms.comment: Literally “drawn tight”: the participle of adstringō (also spelled astringō) used as an adjective of a person close with money. Lewis & Short: “sparing, parsimonious”, not before the Augustan period.

terms.gloss: tight-fisted, holding fast to what one has
evidence: Plaut. Capt. 289: tenāxne pater est ejus?
Cic. Cael. 36: patre parcō ac tenācī (Lewis & Short)
Plaut. Bacch. 401: jūstus injūstus, malignus largus
terms.comment: The opposite of benignus and of largus.

phrases.latin: Quid tū ais? tenāxne pater est ejus? — Immō edepol pertināx.
phrases.english: Tell me, is his father tight-fisted? — Tight? He never lets go at all.

sources: Lewis & Short: sordidus · Lewis & Short: tenax · Lewis & Short: malignus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 157, 158, 394.
